Store the length of the common substring ending exactly at (i, j). What does a match build on, what does a mismatch become, and where does the answer live?
problems.javaNote: The answer is the maximum over all cells, not the bottom-right cell. Keep a separate max variable instead of returning dp[n][m].

problems.title: Longest palindromic subsequence
hints: A palindromic subsequence reads the same forwards and backwards. What happens if you compare the string with its own reverse?
Either reuse a known two-string DP against the reversed string, or do interval DP on (left, right). What should happen when the two ends match versus differ?
problems.javaNote: new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString() is the clean way to reverse; String has no reverse method, and building by += in a loop is O(n^2).

problems.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
hints: The O(n^2) idea asks, for each element, which earlier smaller element gives the longest chain. Among many increasing subsequences of the same length, which one is the most useful to keep extending later?
Maintain a sorted array indexed by subsequence length. What should each slot hold, and how can binary search decide where a new number goes?
problems.javaNote: On a partially filled tails array use Arrays.binarySearch(tails, 0, size, x), and decode the -(insertionPoint) - 1 result correctly; or write your own lower-bound search.

problems.title: Number of Longest Increasing Subsequences
hints: Knowing the LIS length ending at each index is not enough; several different chains can reach the same length. What second number should each index carry?
Carry (length, count) per index. When extending from an earlier element, how should the count change if the chain becomes strictly longer versus exactly ties?
problems.javaNote: Initialize both arrays with Arrays.fill(len, 1) and Arrays.fill(cnt, 1); forgetting the count initialization gives zero for every answer.

problems.title: Edit distance
hints: Look at the last characters of both strings. If they differ, there are exactly three operations that could have fixed that position. What does each one leave behind?
2D DP over prefix lengths. What are the costs of converting to or from an empty string, and which neighbouring cell does each operation correspond to?
problems.javaNote: Remember Math.min takes only two arguments; nest calls for three options. Fill row 0 and column 0 with i and j before the main loops.

problems.title: Wildcard matching
hints: '?' is easy: it matches exactly one character. The trouble is '*'. At each step, a star can either match nothing or swallow one more character. Which subproblems do those two options lead to?
DP over (pattern prefix, text prefix). Be careful with the empty-text base case: when can a non-empty pattern prefix match an empty text?
problems.javaNote: Use a boolean[][] table, and convert strings to char[] first. Recursion without memoization on long inputs risks both TLE and StackOverflowError.

problems.title: Matrix chain multiplication
hints: The final multiplication splits the chain into a left part and a right part at some position. If you knew the best cost of each part, what would the total be?
Interval DP over (i, j). What do you iterate over inside an interval, and in what order must intervals be filled so their subresults are ready?
problems.javaNote: Products of three dimensions can overflow int for large sizes; use long for intermediate cost. Initialize mins with Integer.MAX_VALUE only before comparing, never before adding.

problems.title: Palindrome partitioning II
hints: Checking 'is s[i..j] a palindrome' again and again is the hidden cost. Could you answer that question instantly? And what does the last piece of a partition look like?
Precompute palindrome information once, then a 1D DP over prefixes. What does each prefix's value depend on, given every possible palindromic last piece?
problems.javaNote: Fill the boolean palindrome table so that isPal[i+1][j-1] is already computed before isPal[i][j]; iterating i downward avoids reading uncomputed cells.

problems.title: Trie Implementation and Advanced Operations
hints: You must answer exact-word counts, prefix counts, and support erase. A single end-of-word flag cannot answer 'how many'. What should each node remember?
Each trie node keeps counters instead of a flag. Which two counts answer the two queries, and how do insert and erase adjust them along a path?
problems.javaNote: Use Node[] children = new Node[26] with c - 'a' indexing; a HashMap<Character, Node> works but autoboxes every char and is slower.

problems.title: Longest Word with All Prefixes
hints: A word qualifies only if every one of its prefixes is also a word in the list. Can you check all prefixes of a word in a single walk instead of separate lookups?
Trie with end-of-word markers. While walking a word's path, what must be true at every node for it to qualify? Do not forget the tie-break rule.
problems.javaNote: For lexicographic tie-breaking use a.compareTo(b) < 0; comparing strings with == checks references, not contents, and < does not compile for String.

problems.title: Number of distinct substrings in a string
hints: Every substring is a prefix of some suffix. Storing all substrings in a set costs a lot of memory. Is there a structure where shared prefixes are stored only once?
Insert every suffix into a trie. How does the number of trie nodes relate to the number of distinct substrings, and does the empty string count?
problems.javaNote: Inserting all suffixes creates up to O(n^2) nodes; Node objects with 26-slot arrays add up fast, so watch memory and avoid HashSet<String> of substrings.

problems.title: Maximum XOR of two numbers in an array
hints: A single high bit outweighs all lower bits combined. For a given number, what would you like its partner's bits to look like, starting from the top?
Binary trie over fixed-width bit representations, highest bit first. At each level, which child do you prefer for the current number, and when are you forced otherwise?
problems.javaNote: Extract bits with (num >> i) & 1; don't use Math.pow. With non-negative ints, start from bit 30; including bit 31 is fine but mind sign with >>.

problems.title: Maximum Xor with an element from an array
hints: Each query only allows array elements up to some limit. Rebuilding a structure per query is too slow. Does the order in which you answer queries have to match the input order?
Answer queries offline, ordered by limit, so a binary trie only ever grows. How do you restore input order, and what if no element is allowed yet?
problems.javaNote: Sort query indices with Integer.compare in the comparator (or sort an int[][] by column), and store the original index so answers go back in input order.

problems.title: Rabin Karp Algorithm
hints: Comparing the pattern against every window character by character repeats work. Could a single number summarise a window, and be updated cheaply when it slides?
Rolling hash: how do you remove the outgoing character and add the incoming one in O(1)? Why must you still verify when hashes match?
problems.javaNote: Do the hash arithmetic in long with a modulus, and when removing the outgoing char add the modulus before taking % again; Java's % can return negatives.

problems.title: Z function
hints: If you know how far the string matches its own prefix from earlier positions, can that knowledge skip comparisons at later positions?
Z-array: for each index, how far does the string match its own prefix from there? Keep the rightmost known matching window. How would you join pattern and text to search?
problems.javaNote: Pick a separator character that cannot appear in either string (e.g. '$'), and build the combined string with StringBuilder rather than repeated concatenation.

problems.title: KMP Algorithm or LPS array
hints: When a mismatch happens after several matched characters, the naive approach throws all of that away. Could part of what you matched already be the start of the pattern?
Precompute, for each pattern prefix, the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. On a mismatch, how does that table tell you where to resume instead of restarting?
problems.javaNote: Building the LPS table, the fallback is a while loop (len = lps[len - 1]), not a single if; using if gives subtly wrong tables on patterns like "aabaaab".

problems.title: Shortest Palindrome
hints: You may only add characters at the front, so part of s survives untouched at the start of the answer. Which part can that be, and what must be true of it?
You need the longest palindromic prefix quickly. Could a prefix-function on a string built from s and its reverse find it? Why is a separator needed?
problems.javaNote: Use a separator like '#' between s and its reverse, otherwise the LPS value can extend past the original string's length and give wrong answers.

problems.title: Power Set Bit Manipulation
hints: With n elements, each subset is a yes/no decision per element. How many subsets are there, and what familiar sequence of numbers encodes n yes/no decisions?
Let an integer stand for a subset. How do you enumerate all of them, and how does a single bit decide membership of one element?
problems.javaNote: Use 1 << n, not Math.pow(2, n), which returns double. For n >= 31 an int shift overflows; use 1L << n if n could be large.

problems.title: Single Number - II
hints: Every number except one appears three times. Look at a single bit position across all numbers. What can you say about the count of 1s there?
Count set bits per position and use modulo 3 to rebuild the answer, or keep two bitmasks tracking 'seen once' and 'seen twice'.
problems.javaNote: When rebuilding the answer bit by bit, include bit 31 with ans |= (1 << 31); this correctly restores negative numbers in two's complement.

problems.title: Single Number - III
hints: XOR of everything gives a ^ b for the two unique numbers. Since a != b, that result has at least one 1 bit. What does that bit tell you about a versus b?
Use one bit where a and b differ to divide all numbers into two groups. What does each group then reduce to?
problems.javaNote: Isolate the lowest set bit with x & (-x). If x is Integer.MIN_VALUE, -x equals x, which still works, but don't use Math.abs on it.

problems.title: Find the repeating and missing number
hints: You know exactly which numbers 1..n should be present. Comparing the actual sum (and something else) to the expected one gives equations. How many unknowns are there?
Either form two equations from differences of sums and sums of squares, or XOR with 1..n and separate the two unknowns by a differing bit.
problems.javaNote: Sum of squares up to n overflows int quickly; compute expected sums and differences in long, casting before multiplying (long) n * (n + 1).

problems.title: Print all primes till N
hints: Trial division of every number up to N repeats a lot of work. Once you know a number is prime, what do you immediately know about its multiples?
Sieve of Eratosthenes with a boolean array. From which multiple can marking safely start, and up to which prime do you need to mark at all?
problems.javaNote: Start marking at i * i but compute it as (long) i * i or loop while i <= n / i; i * i overflows int for large N and becomes negative.
